LICCERT.TITLE: NCCPA Certification
LICCERT.ORG: National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants
LICCERT.DESC: NCCPA is the only certifying organization for PAs in the United States. Established as a not-for-profit organization in 1974, NCCPA provides certification programs that reflect standards for clinical knowledge, clinical reasoning and other medical skills and professional behaviors required upon entry into practice and throughout the careers of PAs.

LICCERT.TITLE: Physician Assistant License
LICCERT.DESC: The Texas Physician Assistant Board issues a physician assistant license to qualified individuals to practice in Texas. In addition to a license, physician assistants in Texas must practice under the supervision of one or more supervising physicians, and if prescribing drugs, must have a prescriptive delegation agreement with their supervising physician(s). The Licensure Department of the Texas Physician Assistant Board is committed to furthering the mission of the Board by ensuring quality healthcare for the citizens of Texas by upholding the standards set in statute and Board Rule, and by efficiently processing licensure applications.

LICCERT.TITLE: Basic Life Support Provider
LICCERT.DESC: The American Heart Association's Basic Life Support (BLS) course trains participants to promptly recognize several life-threatening emergencies, give high-quality chest compressions, deliver appropriate ventilations and provide early use of an AED. Reflects science and education from the American Heart Association Guidelines Update for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (ECC).

MEMBER.NAME: PA Education Association

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: A final lecture was provided covering the regional anatomical topic of the abdomen for the didactic course PHAS 5202 Human Anatomy and Radiology II of the PA department. In this last lecture of the abdomen module, an IRAT was provided at the beginning of lecture followed by a discourse concerning the diaphragm, nerves and musculature of the posterior abdominal wall, and autonomic innervation of abdominal viscera. Clinical correlations included referred pain from the diaphragm, types of hiatal hernias, and posterior abdominal pain.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: A third lecture was provided covering the regional anatomical topic of the abdomen for the didactic course PHAS 5202 Human Anatomy and Radiology II of the PA department. For this lecture, an IRAT was administered at the beginning of lecture followed by a detailed discussion of the spleen, pancreas, liver, biliary ducts, gallbladder, portal-systemic anastomoses, kidneys, and suprarenal glands. Some clinical correlations provided included rupture of the spleen, pancreatic cancer, cirrhosis of the liver, and cholecystitis.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: Once again, served as a guest lecturer covering the regional anatomical topic of the abdomen for the didactic course PHAS 5202 Human Anatomy and Radiology II of the PA department. In this second lecture, an IRAT was given to the students at the beginning of lecture followed by a discussion of the abdominal peritoneum, peritoneal cavity, and abdominal viscera. The esophagus, stomach, small intestines, and large intestine were the abdominal organs of focus in this lecture. Clinical correlations including peritonitis, ascites, pyloric stenosis, and appendicitis were also discussed.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: As a guest lecturer, I provided an initial lecture covering the regional anatomical topic of the abdomen for the didactic course PHAS 5202 Human Anatomy and Radiology II of the PA department. For this lecture, an IRAT was given at the beginning of lecture following by an in depth explanation of the layers, musculature, innervation, arterial supply, and lymphatic drainage of the anterolateral abdominal wall. Clinical correlations were provided with a particular emphasis on inguinal hernias.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: Provided a third and final lecture concerning the regional anatomical topic of the back for the didactic course PHAS 5201 Human Anatomy and Radiology I of the PA department. For this lecture the spinal cord, spinal meninges, spinal roots, and spinal nerves and rami were covered in detail. Helpful mnemonics were provided once again to enhance understanding of this lecture material. Thereafter, I conducted a formal review of my previous lectures regarding the anatomy of the back and provided a study guide to our students to aid their exam preparation.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: Once again, served as a guest lecturer covering the regional anatomical topic of the back for the didactic course PHAS 5201 Human Anatomy and Radiology I of the PA department. For this second lecture, an IRAT was given to the students at the start of lecture. Thereafter, I explained in depth the extrinsic and intrinsic back muscles including layers, origins, insertions, and function. Mnemonics were provided to help reinforce comprehension of the lecture content. The suboccipital muscles, suboccipital triangle, and deep neck muscles were discussed as well.

NCTEACH.AUDIENCE: Internal to The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
NCTEACH.DESC: Served as a guest lecturer covering the regional anatomical topic of the back for the didactic course PHAS 5201 Human Anatomy and Radiology I of the PA department. For my lecture on this day, I began with an IRAT at the start of class and proceeded with discussing surface anatomy, cutaneous innervation, osteology, the vertebral column, specific vertebral characteristics, vertebral articulations, and vertebral ligaments and joints. Clinical correlations were included in my lecture along with a video demonstrating key clinical findings when assessing for scoliosis.
